body: Welcome. Over about ninety days you will get one short note a day to help you become the kind of friend people can count on, in small, steady ways.
Start by listing three friends you have meant to contact for a while. You do not need to message them yet; just let the names come to mind.
Being a reliable friend is not about grand gestures. It is mostly about small promises kept and replies that do not take a month.
Notice what usually stops you from getting in touch. Is it tiredness, guilt about the silence, or not knowing what to say?
Send one friend a short message today with no question attached. Something like, I saw this and thought of you, is plenty.
If you owe someone a reply, answer it today, even briefly. A late reply is still far warmer than none at all.
Write your friends' birthdays somewhere you will actually see them. Remembering is easier when you do not rely on memory alone.
Think of a friend who always shows up for you. What exactly do they do? Pick one of their habits to borrow this week.
Before you say yes to plans, check that you can truly make them. A smaller yes you keep beats a bigger one you cancel.
When you must cancel, do it early and suggest a new date in the same message. That turns a let-down into a postponement.
Arrive on time for the next thing you have arranged with a friend. Punctuality quietly says, you matter to me.
Ask a friend how something they mentioned last time turned out. Following up shows you were really listening.
Keep a short note on your phone of things friends are going through: an interview, a move, a hospital visit. Check it weekly.
Reliability grows from routines. Choose one regular slot, such as Sunday evenings, for catching up with people.
Call rather than text one friend this week. Hearing a voice can mean more than a dozen quick messages.
If guilt about a long silence is stopping you, simply say, I have been rubbish at keeping in touch, and I have missed you. Most people are glad.
Offer one specific kind of help today. Can I bring dinner on Thursday is easier to accept than let me know if you need anything.
Notice which friendships you only maintain when it suits you. Is there one you could tend even when nothing is in it for you?
Showing up includes the dull bits: helping someone move, waiting with them at an appointment, picking them up from the station.
Put the next catch-up in the diary before you say goodbye. Plans made in person are far more likely to happen.
When a friend shares good news, celebrate it properly. Being reliable in joy matters as much as being reliable in trouble.
Think about how quickly you usually reply to friends compared with work emails. Could friends get a little of that promptness?
Today, keep one tiny promise to a friend that you might normally let slide, like sending the recipe or the link you mentioned.
If a friend goes quiet, check in gently. A short message saying you are thinking of them can mean a great deal.
You do not need to be available all the time to be dependable. You just need to be consistent in what you do offer.
Notice how you feel after you have kept your word to a friend. That quiet satisfaction is worth remembering.
Ask one friend what kind of support they like when life is hard. Some want advice, some want company, some want distraction.
Write a short card or letter to a friend this week. Something they can hold often stays with them for years.
When you are with a friend, put your phone away. Being fully present is a form of showing up.
Look back over the past month. Which friend did you show up for, and how did it go?
Be honest about your limits. Saying I cannot do Saturday, but I can call on Friday, keeps trust intact.
Notice any friend you tend to keep at arm's length. Is there a small step you could take towards them?
If you said you would do something and forgot, own it simply. Sorry, I dropped that, I will sort it today, repairs a lot.
Remember the anniversaries that are hard for your friends, such as the date someone they loved died. A message that day is rarely forgotten.
Show up for a friend's thing even if it is not your thing: their gig, their match, their exhibition, their child's play.
Reliable friends are not perfect friends. They simply come back, again and again, after the gaps.
Pick one friendship that has drifted and suggest a low-effort plan, such as a walk or a coffee near their home.
Make it easy for friends to see you. Offer to travel to them, or choose somewhere that suits their schedule.
Pay attention to friends who always do the organising. This time, be the one who sends the invitation.
When a friend is struggling, you do not need perfect words. I am here, and I am not going anywhere, is often enough.
Notice whether you only reach out when you need something. Send one message this week that asks for nothing.
Keep a small stash of cards and stamps at home. Being ready makes thoughtful gestures much easier.
Check your calendar for the coming fortnight. Is there a slot you could protect for a friend?
Halfway through. Which small habit has made you a more dependable friend so far? Keep that one going.
Being on time, replying, remembering and following up: these four habits carry most of what reliability means.
Think of a friend who has let you down. Can you hold some grace for them, as you hope others will for you?
If you are going to be late, let your friend know before the time you were due, not after. It is a small courtesy that builds trust.
Offer to be someone's emergency contact, or ask a friend to be yours. Naming that trust can deepen a friendship.
Notice which friends live alone. A regular call or visit can matter more to them than you might guess.
Return something you have borrowed from a friend this week, whether a book, a dish or a jumper.
Remember small preferences: how a friend takes their tea, the food they cannot eat, the song they love. Details show care.
When a friend moves house or starts a new job, check in after the first week. Transitions can be lonely.
Try a standing date with one friend: the first Monday of the month, a weekly call, a yearly trip. Rhythm makes showing up automatic.
If you are going through a hard time yourself, let a friend know. Reliability also means letting people in.
Notice when you are tempted to flake because you feel tired. Often a short visit still leaves you both glad you went.
Reply to the group chat with something warm, not just a thumbs up. Small effort keeps a circle alive.
Think of what you would want from a friend if your life fell apart. Could you offer that to someone now?
Write down the names of the people you would drop everything for. Do they know it?
Practise saying, I will get back to you by tomorrow, and then doing exactly that.
When a friend has a baby, an illness or a bereavement, the help is often needed most after the first rush of messages ends.
Notice whether you hold grudges about friends who have been less reliable than you. Let one go, if you can.
Arrange a get-together that brings two of your friends together. Sharing your people is a kind of generosity.
Look out for a friend's quiet milestone: a year sober, a finished course, a hard first month done. Mark it with them.
Being dependable also means being discreet. Keep what friends tell you in confidence to yourself.
If you have let a friendship slide for years, a short message still counts. It is rarely too late to begin again.
Ask a friend, is there anything I could do better as your friend? Listen without defending yourself.
Notice how your reliability affects your own sense of self. Keeping your word to others builds respect for yourself too.
When plans change on their side, be gracious. Being easy to rearrange with is part of being a good friend.
Check in on a friend who always seems fine. Strong people need someone to show up for them as well.
Make a small, practical gesture this week: drop round soup, water their plants, collect a parcel.
Think about the friends who knew you years ago. Could you send one a memory you share?
Remember that showing up looks different in different seasons. A new parent's friendship might be a five-minute voice note.
Notice the friendships that feel one-sided. Talk about it kindly rather than quietly withdrawing.
Look at your past week. Did you keep the promises you made to friends? Celebrate the ones you did.
Invite a newer friend into something you usually do with old friends. Reliability helps new friendships take root.
If a friend says, do not worry about it, still do the small thing you offered. Follow-through is what they remember.
When you hear a friend is unwell, act quickly. A message within a day says you were paying attention.
Write a thank-you to a friend who showed up for you in the past. Naming it often surprises and moves them.
Notice how much easier it has become to reach out. The awkwardness fades with practice.
Keep your promises to friends in the same place you keep work deadlines. They deserve the same care.
Think of one friend you could check on every week, without fail, for the next month.
When you cannot be there in person, find another way: a call, a delivery, a card, a playlist.
Showing up is a habit, not a mood. You have been practising it for almost three months now.
Picture your friends describing you. Would they say you are someone they can count on? What would you like them to say?
Plan one small surprise for a friend this month, something that says, I remembered.
Share what you have learnt about friendship with someone who feels lonely. Your example may help them reach out too.
Look at the routines you have built: the birthday list, the regular slot, the follow-up notes. Choose the ones you will keep for good.
Notice the friendships that have grown warmer over these weeks. Steady care quietly changes things.
Look back over these ninety days. Which moment of showing up are you proudest of?
Friends rarely remember the perfect thing you said. They remember that you came, and that you kept coming.
You began with a list of people you had meant to contact. Now reaching out is part of how you live.
This is the last note. You have become someone your friends can count on, and that steadiness is a gift you can keep giving.
